questions.question: Your team misses a sprint goal partly due to your delayed task. What is the best response in the retrospective?
options: Own your part and suggest how to avoid it next time
Point out others who were also late
Stay quiet to avoid attention
Say the goal was unrealistic anyway
questions.explanation: Taking ownership and proposing improvements builds trust and helps the team learn.

questions.question: You accepted a task in stand-up but realise you lack time. What should you do?
options: Do a rushed version without telling anyone
Hope no one notices the delay
Hand it to a junior without informing the team
Tell the team early so the task can be reassigned or re-planned
questions.explanation: Being transparent about commitments lets the team adjust plans and remain reliable.

questions.question: A new teammate struggles with the project setup. You have some spare time. What is best?
options: Tell them to read the docs and leave
Do it for them silently on their laptop
Offer to pair with them and walk through it
Report their slowness to the manager
questions.explanation: Pairing helps them learn, speeds onboarding and strengthens team cohesion.

questions.question: In a Scrum team, who is primarily responsible for prioritising the product backlog?
options: The Scrum Master
The Product Owner
The newest developer
The QA tester
questions.explanation: According to the Scrum Guide, the Product Owner is accountable for ordering the Product Backlog.

questions.question: You notice a bug in code written by a teammate. What is the best action?
options: Let them know politely and offer to help fix it
Fix it silently and say nothing
Mention it in a public channel to warn others
Ignore it because it is not your code
questions.explanation: Respectful, direct communication keeps the owner informed and encourages shared ownership.

questions.question: A quiet teammate rarely speaks in meetings. What is a good way to include them?
options: Assume they have nothing to add
Ask them to speak first every time to test them
Ignore them since others are more active
Invite their input on topics in their expertise
questions.explanation: Inviting contributions respectfully helps quieter members participate and adds diverse perspectives.

questions.question: A feature succeeded thanks to a teammate's key idea. In the demo, what should you do?
options: Present it as your own idea
Credit only the manager
Acknowledge their contribution explicitly
Avoid mentioning anyone's name
questions.explanation: Giving credit fairly builds trust and motivation within the team.

questions.question: Before merging your changes to the shared main branch, what is good team practice?
options: Push directly to main to save time
Open a pull request for review and ensure tests pass
Merge late at night to avoid conflicts
Delete others' changes that conflict with yours
questions.explanation: Code review and passing tests protect the shared codebase and spread knowledge.

questions.question: Two teammates disagree about which database to use, stalling work. What is the best way forward?
options: Agree on criteria, compare options against them, then decide
Let the loudest person decide
Use both databases to avoid choosing
Postpone the decision indefinitely
questions.explanation: Objective criteria depersonalise the conflict and lead to a reasoned decision.

questions.question: You accidentally deleted a test database. What is the best action?
options: Hide it and hope backups run
Blame a script someone else wrote
Wait until someone notices
Report it immediately and help restore it
questions.explanation: Prompt honesty limits damage and supports a culture where mistakes can be fixed and learned from.

questions.question: Which leader behaviour best promotes psychological safety in a team?
options: Publicly naming people who make errors
Only praising those who never ask questions
Responding to mistakes with curiosity rather than blame
Making decisions without team input
questions.explanation: Research on team effectiveness links psychological safety to leaders treating errors as learning opportunities.

questions.question: Your distributed team struggles with missed handoffs between time zones. What helps most?
options: Expect everyone to be online at the same time
Written handoff notes in a shared tracker at the end of each day
Use private chats for each handoff
Rely on memory and quick calls
questions.explanation: Structured async handoffs keep work visible and continuous across time zones.

questions.question: You finish your sprint tasks early while a teammate is overloaded. What is best?
options: Offer to take on some of their tasks after checking with the team
Start a new personal side project
Wait quietly for the next sprint
Take their tasks without asking anyone
questions.explanation: Proactively helping, coordinated with the team, improves team delivery.

questions.question: A teammate keeps missing code review requests, slowing you down. What is the best first step?
options: Complain about them in the team channel
Escalate to the manager immediately
Stop requesting their reviews entirely
Talk to them privately, describe the impact and ask how to fix it
questions.explanation: Direct, private, impact-focused conversation is the most respectful first step before escalation.

questions.question: A team keeps arguing about meeting times and response expectations. What helps most?
options: Let each person follow their own rules
Have the newest member decide
Create a shared working agreement the team defines together
Stop holding meetings at all
questions.explanation: A team-created working agreement sets shared norms and reduces recurring friction.

questions.question: The team chooses an approach you argued against. What is the best behaviour?
options: Quietly implement your own approach
Commit fully to the decision while noting your concerns for review
Do the minimum to prove you were right
Keep reopening the debate in every meeting
questions.explanation: 'Disagree and commit' allows healthy debate while preserving team execution.

questions.question: Two colleagues have an ongoing personal conflict affecting the team's delivery. As team lead, what is the best approach?
options: Meet them, focus on behaviours and impact, and agree on norms
Ignore it as long as tasks finish
Move one of them off the team immediately
Discuss the conflict with the whole team in their absence
questions.explanation: Addressing behaviour and impact with the people involved, and agreeing norms, resolves conflict fairly.

questions.question: A new team is having frequent disagreements over roles and approach. In Tuckman's model, which stage is this?
options: Forming
Norming
Performing
Storming
questions.explanation: Storming is characterised by conflict as members assert ideas and negotiate roles.

questions.question: Retrospectives keep producing the same complaints with no change. What is the most effective fix?
options: Stop holding retrospectives
Make retros longer to discuss more issues
Pick one or two actions with owners and review them next retro
Only let the manager speak in retros
questions.explanation: Limited, owned, followed-up action items turn retrospectives into real improvement.

questions.question: Your feature depends on the design team, which has different priorities. What is the best way to collaborate?
options: Build without designs and fix later
Align early on shared goals and agree timelines with them
Escalate to senior management immediately
Assume they will deliver when needed
questions.explanation: Early alignment and explicit agreements on dependencies reduce delays across teams.

questions.question: Only one engineer understands the deployment process. What is the best team action?
options: Document it and rotate others through deployments
Keep relying on that engineer
Forbid deployments when they are away
Rewrite the process from scratch immediately
questions.explanation: Documentation and rotation reduce single-person dependency (bus factor) and spread knowledge.

questions.question: Your lead often changes priorities mid-sprint, causing rework. What is the best approach?
options: Complain to other teams about the lead
Ignore new priorities and continue your plan
Raise it angrily in the sprint review
Share the impact privately with examples and suggest a change process
questions.explanation: Specific, private, solution-oriented feedback is the most constructive way to address issues with a lead.
